claims.text: Replacing conventional EAM references with a machine-learning interatomic potential will improve reference–target phase-space overlap in multicomponent high-entropy alloys near melting.
Replacing EAM references with an MLIP will significantly reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The proposed method applies to equiatomic multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both solid and liquid states.
The applicable temperature interval is approximately 0.9–1.1 times the melting temperature.
The MLIP should be trained extensively on ab initio molecular-dynamics configurations representing the liquid state.
High-temperature liquid high-entropy alloys exhibit high configurational diversity.
Elemental and binary benchmarks should be used to calibrate and validate the MLIP.
An MLIP trained on diverse liquid configurations will describe the possible liquid atomic arrangements more accurately than a traditional EAM potential.
Training on diverse ab initio liquid configurations enables the MLIP to capture complex many-body interactions and varied atomic environments.
Greater fidelity to many-body liquid environments makes the MLIP reference phase space better match the target ab initio phase space.
Improved reference–target phase-space overlap reduces TI path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD calculations using conventional EAM references.
Using the MLIP reference will improve solid–liquid free-energy estimates relative to EAM-reference calculations.
The reduction in TI path mismatch may be on the order of tens of percent.
TOR-TILD calculations with conventional EAM potentials constitute the baseline.
The expected improvement may not generalize to non-equiatomic compositions or systems with substantially different melting behavior.
The exact quantitative reduction in TI path mismatch cannot be established without systematic benchmarking.
A deep neural-network potential has been used to describe both solid and liquid states and predict melting behavior in the high-entropy carbonitride system (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x.
Parallel EAM-reference and MLIP-reference TI calculations can test the proposed improvement by comparing path mismatch, convergence, phase-space overlap, and phase free-energy differences.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in phase-space overlap and TI path mismatch would falsify the hypothesis.
